artworks.title: The Mark Twain House
artworks.description: Sam and Olivia (Livy) Clemens built this 25-room, three-floor house of brick and brownstone in 1873–74 and lived here with their daughters Susy, Clara and Jean from 1874 to 1891, what Mark Twain called the happiest and most productive years of his life. Here he wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, The Prince and the Pauper, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court. The house was shown only by guided tour; the photo shows the east (front) side.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: The Mark Twain House (1874): guided tours only. Pick floor B, 1, 2 or 3 above to see its rooms
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The street side and the service wing
artworks.description: The side facing Farmington Avenue, with the service wing: the kitchen, the butler’s pantry and the servants’ rooms, where the butler George Griffin, the cook, the maids and the nurse worked. Its gables, balconies and porches gave the house its nickname as a “Mississippi steamboat”.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: The Mark Twain House (1874): guided tours only. Pick floor B, 1, 2 or 3 above to see its rooms
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The Carriage House
artworks.description: The Clemenses’ stable and carriage house. The coachman Patrick McAleer, their highest-paid servant, lived upstairs with his wife and children; Twain called him his idea of “an ideal gentleman”. Today the hayloft holds offices and the barn floor is a rental hall, so it is not part of the tour.
artworks.imageCredit: Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: The Clemenses’ Carriage House (1874), where the coachman Patrick McAleer lived with his family: not open to the public (offices and a rental hall)
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The porte-cochère
artworks.description: Carriages drove up the hill from Farmington Avenue and under this covered entrance, so guests could step out of the rain at the front door. Tours go into the house here.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Porte-cochère and the front steps, where tours go in
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The Ombra
artworks.description: The large covered porch the family called the Ombra (Italian for “shade”). In summer it was an outdoor living room; the carriage drive ran alongside it to the Carriage House.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: The Ombra (Italian for “shade”): the big covered porch
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The Entrance Hall
artworks.artist: Louis C. Tiffany & Co., Associated Artists
artworks.description: In 1881 the Clemenses hired Louis C. Tiffany’s firm, Associated Artists, to decorate the newly enlarged hall and the main rooms. The dark red walls and ceiling are covered with silver-stencilled patterns inspired by Morocco, India, Japan, China and Turkey. The same year, the firm redecorated the state rooms of the White House.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Entrance Hall: Associated Artists’ 1881 stencils, the carved staircase and the fireplace
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Fireplace of the Entrance Hall
artworks.artist: Louis C. Tiffany & Co., Associated Artists
artworks.description: The fireplace on the north wall of the hall, framed by Associated Artists’ carved woodwork and stencilling.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Entrance Hall: Associated Artists’ 1881 stencils, the carved staircase and the fireplace
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The main staircase
artworks.description: The carved staircase rises from the south-west corner of the hall to the second and third floors. The house has no elevator: a full tour climbs 41 steps to the Billiard Room.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Entrance Hall: Associated Artists’ 1881 stencils, the carved staircase and the fireplace
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Newel post with lamps
artworks.artist: Louis C. Tiffany & Co., Associated Artists
artworks.description: The lamps on the newel post at the foot of the staircase. The house had the latest comforts of the 1870s: gas light, central heating, plumbing, a burglar alarm, speaking tubes and one of the first private telephones in Hartford.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Entrance Hall: Associated Artists’ 1881 stencils, the carved staircase and the fireplace
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Bust of Samuel Clemens
artworks.description: A bust of Samuel Clemens in the hall, in front of the stencilled walls.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Entrance Hall: Associated Artists’ 1881 stencils, the carved staircase and the fireplace
artworks.placeNote: In the room the museum’s exhibit page names; the place of the room is our guess.

artworks.title: The Drawing Room
artworks.artist: Louis C. Tiffany & Co., Associated Artists
artworks.description: The formal parlour where Livy received callers and the family put on plays and charades. Associated Artists decorated it with pale walls and stencilling inspired by India.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Drawing Room
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Drawing Room fireplace
artworks.artist: Louis C. Tiffany & Co., Associated Artists
artworks.description: The south wall of the Drawing Room with its fireplace.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Drawing Room
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The Dining Room
artworks.artist: Louis C. Tiffany & Co., Associated Artists
artworks.description: Where the Clemenses entertained guests such as William Dean Howells. The walls are covered with embossed, gilded paper chosen by Associated Artists.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Dining Room
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The window above the fireplace
artworks.description: The chimney of the Dining Room splits around a window, so the family could watch the snow falling outside right above the flames of the fire.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Dining Room
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The Library and its Scottish mantel
artworks.description: The family’s favourite room. The carved wooden mantel came from Ayton Castle in Scotland; the Clemenses bought it on their travels in 1879. Twain made up stories for his daughters that had to include every object on the mantel, in order, from the painting at one end to the one at the other.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Library, with the carved Scottish mantel
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The Library alcove
artworks.description: The bay window alcove on the west side of the Library, looking out over the hill where the Park River once ran.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Library, with the carved Scottish mantel
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The Conservatory
artworks.description: Opening off the Library, the glass conservatory has a fountain and a marble-chip floor and is filled with plants, kept today by UConn Master Gardeners. The Clemens girls called it “the Jungle”.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Conservatory, with its fountain (the girls called it “the Jungle”)
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The Mahogany Guest Room
artworks.description: The first-floor guest room, with its own dressing room and bathroom, so important guests did not have to climb the stairs.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Mahogany Guest Room
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Speaking tube to the kitchen
artworks.description: The mouthpiece of a speaking tube: guests could talk straight to the kitchen and ask the servants for what they needed.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Mahogany Guest Room
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Dressing Room of the guest suite
artworks.description: The dressing room of the first-floor guest suite.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Dressing Room of the guest suite
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Bathroom of the guest suite
artworks.description: The guest bathroom, with running water: a luxury in the 1870s. The house had several bathrooms with flush toilets.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Bathroom of the guest suite
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The second-floor stair hall
artworks.description: The second-floor hall at the top of the main staircase, which leads to the family’s bedrooms.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Upper hall, over the Entrance Hall
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Mr. and Mrs. Clemens’ bedroom and the Venetian bed
artworks.description: The carved bed, with angels on the posts and headboard, was bought in Venice in 1878. The Clemenses slept with their heads at the foot of the bed so they could look at the carving. The girls were allowed to take down the small angels and play with them.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Mr. and Mrs. Clemens’ Bedroom
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Gas “cord” to a lamp
artworks.description: A flexible tube carried gas from the ceiling gasolier to a lamp beside the bed: the latest thing in home lighting before electricity.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Mr. and Mrs. Clemens’ Bedroom
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The Langdon Guest Room
artworks.description: A second-floor guest room.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Langdon Guest Room
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Second-floor bathroom
artworks.description: A bathroom on the west side of the second floor, with its tub.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Bathroom (west side)
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The School Room
artworks.description: Twain first used this room as his study; then it became the schoolroom where Susy, Clara and Jean had their lessons with a governess, and Twain moved his writing up to the Billiard Room.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: School Room: the girls’ schoolroom
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: South-east bathroom
artworks.description: The bathroom in the south-east corner of the second floor.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Bathroom (south-east corner)
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Clara and Jean’s Bedroom
artworks.description: The bedroom of the two younger daughters, Clara (born 1874) and Jean (born 1880), with its fireplace.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Clara and Jean’s Bedroom
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Susy’s Bedroom
artworks.description: The room of the eldest daughter, Susy, who at 13 wrote a biography of her father (“We are a very happy family!”). She died of meningitis in this house in 1896, aged 24, while her parents were abroad.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Susy’s Bedroom
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The third-floor stair hall
artworks.description: The hall at the top of the stairs, leading to the Billiard Room, the guest room, the servants’ room and the Texas deck.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Third-floor hall
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The Billiard Room, Mark Twain’s study
artworks.description: Twain’s private hideaway, where he played billiards with friends, smoked and wrote: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn was finished here. The ceiling is stencilled with crossed billiard cues, pipes and cigars.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Billiard Room: Mark Twain’s study, where he wrote Huckleberry Finn
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Carved marble window
artworks.description: A translucent, carved marble window in the south wall of the Billiard Room.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: Billiard Room: Mark Twain’s study, where he wrote Huckleberry Finn
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: The Texas deck
artworks.description: A third-floor porch named after the “Texas deck”, the top deck of a Mississippi steamboat, where the pilot and the officers lived: a nod to Twain’s years as a river pilot.
artworks.imageCredit: Jack E. Boucher, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain
artworks.galleryName: The “Texas deck”: a porch named after the top deck of a Mississippi steamboat
artworks.placeNote: Room from the Historic American Buildings Survey photo caption.

artworks.title: Mark Twain: I have sampled this life
artworks.description: The life and work of Samuel Clemens (1835–1910): journalist, lecturer, entrepreneur, inventor and one of the most celebrated American writers. On view: first editions of his books, spectacles he wore, and the Paige Compositor.
artworks.imageCredit: Mark Twain (Library of Congress), not a photo of the exhibit
artworks.galleryName: Aetna Gallery: “Mark Twain: I have sampled this life” and the Paige Compositor
artworks.placeNote: In the room the museum’s exhibit page names; the place of the room is our guess.

artworks.title: The Paige Compositor
artworks.description: A typesetting machine meant to set type automatically. Twain poured a fortune into it; only two were ever fully built and neither went beyond testing. This is the only one left. A newspaper called it “marvelously ingenious… worthless commercially, the costliest machine ever built.”
artworks.imageCredit: The Mark Twain House & Museum
artworks.galleryName: Aetna Gallery: “Mark Twain: I have sampled this life” and the Paige Compositor
artworks.placeNote: In the room the museum’s exhibit page names; the place of the room is our guess.

artworks.title: Mark Twain Bench
artworks.description: A bronze bench where you can sit next to Mark Twain (and take a selfie, #SittingWithSam). Donated in memory of Alexander “Sandy” Gaston (1946–2021).
artworks.imageCredit: The Mark Twain House & Museum
artworks.galleryName: Entrance Hall: tickets, the introduction panels, the Mark Twain bench and LEGO Mark Twain; every tour starts here

artworks.title: Suffield Elm Bench
artworks.description: A bench made from the largest American elm in Connecticut, which grew on a farm in Suffield and came down in 2009. The makers counted 148 growth rings.
artworks.galleryName: Second-floor hallway
artworks.placeNote: In the room the museum’s exhibit page names; the place of the room is our guess.

artworks.title: Untitled (Mark Twain’s Birth and Death Places)
artworks.description: Two paintings: the small farmhouse in Florida, Missouri, where Samuel Clemens was born, and Stormfield, the mansion in Redding, Connecticut, where he died. Bontorno was caretaker of Quarry Farm in Elmira, New York, where the Clemenses spent their summers. Oil on cloth; gift of Patty and John Pascal.
artworks.imageCredit: The Mark Twain House & Museum
